newsitem.title: USA: DC may issue debt backed by unpaid parking tickets.
newsitem.headline: DC may issue debt backed by unpaid parking tickets.

text.p: District of Columbia finance officials are studying a novel way of bolstering city revenues by issuing securities backed by unpaid parking tickets, said Thomas Huestis, the city's deputy finance chief.
"A lot of people nationwide are starting to talk about parking tickets as a viable securitization," Huestis said in a telephone interview with Reuters.
He explained that the city would set aside a specific amount of unpaid parking ticket accounts that it currently has on its books.

It would then issue a smaller dollar amount of bonds than total upaid tickets, set up a rigorous system for collecting on those tickets, and then repay the bonds, said Huestis, who was unsure whether any U.S. city has completed such a securitization to date.

Huestis said it is unclear whether the city would issues the bonds this year. He added unpaid parking tickets are only one of a variety of "accounts receivable" the city is eyeing for securitiziation.
D.C. conducted a $25.8 million securitization of delinquent city tax liens in mid-November. Similar deals have been done by Jersey City, N.J., New Haven, Conn., and New York City.

In other upcoming bond deals, Huestis said D.C. will request underwriting proposals from bond firms this week for two short-term negotiated note offerings totaling roughly $274 million set for June to help shore up city cash flow.
A $74 million in budget notes maturing Sept. 30, 1998 would help cover the city's fiscal year 1997 deficit, he said.
Another $200 million tax and revenue anticipation note deal due Sept. 30, 1997 would buttress other city cash flow needs, Huestis said.
Huestis said the city also is targeting competitive sale of $150 million in general obligation bonds for mid May. No sale date has been set, he said.
City officials last fall said they were very pleased with the results of an October 3 competitive offering of $168.8 million of GOs, won by a 16-member underwriting syndicate led by Merrill Lynch.
It was the first time D.C. issued long-term bonds since the city was downgraded to "non-investment grade" ratings by all three major rating agencies in 1995.
